d.title: What the model actually returned
d.caption: Five tokens in, 50,257 scores out. Three things in this table are worth more than any parameter documentation. **Every logit is negative** — they run from −129.87 to −100.25, so their absolute values are an artefact of the final linear layer and mean nothing on their own. The *differences* are everything. And the eight most likely tokens together hold only 0.3202 of the mass, so the other 50,249 carry two thirds of it — which is the entire reason top-p and top-k exist.

d.title: Temperature, read as 'how many tokens is it choosing from'
d.caption: "0.7 is more creative than 0.2" is vague. *The model is choosing from 62 plausible tokens instead of 2* is not. Entropy is the compact version of the same reading and is worth logging in production: a sudden drop means the model has become more certain than the task warrants. Note that **nothing is removed at any setting** — a token at 10⁻⁹ is still reachable, just not in your lifetime.

d.title: Why top-p is the one to reach for
d.caption: Top-k keeps a fixed **count** and top-p keeps a fixed **mass**, and the difference is everything. Across the same four temperatures top-k holds stubbornly at 50 while top-p ranges from 2 to 8,841 — it adapts to how confident the model actually is. That is also why providers tell you to move temperature *or* top-p and not both: top-p's cut depends on the distribution temperature just reshaped, so the two are not independent knobs.

d.title: The only stage with a memory
d.caption: The first three stages see the logit vector and nothing else — given the same vector they do the same thing whether it arrived at step 1 or step 400. Penalties are different: they read what has already been generated and push those tokens' logits down. With the context `The capital of France is`, a presence penalty of 1.0 moves exactly five logits down by 1.0, and `' Paris'` is not one of them, so it stays at −101.2143.

nodes.label: And the penalised set only grows

d.title: Greedy returns the most likely token, not the right one
d.caption: The prompt is `The capital of France is`. The answer is Paris. GPT-2 ranks `' Paris'` **fifth** at 0.032245, so greedy decoding returns `' the'` — every single time, and goes on to produce *"the capital of the French Republic"*. Sampling at 0.7 reaches Paris 9 times in 200 draws. Determinism and correctness are different properties, and `temperature=0` buys you only the first.

d.title: The whole module, as one pass over a logit vector
d.caption: Two columns settle most of the confusion about these parameters. Only top-k and top-p **remove** candidates; temperature and the penalties merely rescale, so no setting of them can make a token unreachable. And only the penalties and the stop conditions look at what has already been generated — which is why they are the two that behave differently at token 400 than at token 1.

d.title: The ratio identity, checked rather than asserted
d.caption: Take any two tokens. Their probability ratio after temperature is `exp((z_a − z_b) / τ)` — the normalising sum cancels, so the ratio depends on **only the gap between the two logits and τ**, never on the other 50,255 entries. Here A and B are one logit apart, so the ratio should be exactly `exp(1/τ)`, and it is, to every digit shown. Temperature does not act on probabilities; it acts on logit gaps.

d.title: The same prompt at five temperatures
d.caption: Distributions are the mechanism; text is what anyone actually judges. The honest version of the advice is in this ladder. At 0.0 the model restates the prompt and then repeats itself verbatim — a loop, not an answer. 0.3 is still largely a restatement. 0.7 is the first setting that *goes somewhere*. 1.0 has started drifting, and 1.4 has stopped tracking the prompt at all.

d.title: The published ranges, and what each is really saying
d.caption: These encode what people converged on rather than anything derived, so treat them as a starting point. For a task not in the table, the useful question is not "how creative should this be" — it is **do I want variety across repeated calls with the same input?** If the answer is no, go low. If the answer is yes, go high and filter afterwards.
cells: one right answer, wanted every time
repetition across turns is the risk

d.title: Zero is a branch, not a limit
d.caption: τ = 0 would divide by zero, so no server computes it. `temperature=0` instead **skips the sampler entirely** and returns the argmax — a different code path, not the end of a continuum. That is why it is reproducible without a seed, and also why reproducibility stops at the model version: the argmax of a slightly different set of weights is a different token, and nothing in your request changed.

nodes.label: But only within a model version

d.title: Top-k keeps a count, whatever the distribution looks like
d.caption: The cut is `k` tokens, always, and that is the flaw. When the model is confident — a peaked distribution — `top_k=50` keeps 49 tokens with almost no mass, and they can still be drawn. When the model is genuinely uncertain across hundreds of reasonable continuations, the same 50 **throws real candidates away**. The count is fixed; the distribution is not.

nodes.label: Which is the argument for top-p
nodes.sub: a mass adapts; a count cannot

d.title: Top-p, worked through five tokens
d.caption: Sort by probability, accumulate from the top, and keep the smallest set whose cumulative mass reaches `p`. The boundary is the part worth being precise about: C's cumulative is **0.90 exactly**, which reaches the threshold, so C is kept and D is the first to go. The set is whatever it takes to cover the mass — three tokens here, two at a sharper temperature, thousands at a flatter one.

d.title: The edge values, and the three that secretly mean greedy
d.caption: Measured on GPT-2's 50,257 tokens, `top_p=0.90` keeps 1,503, `0.95` keeps 3,119, `0.99` keeps 9,144 and `1.00` keeps 38,597 — so even "no truncation" quietly drops the 11,660 tokens with no representable mass. The rows to watch are the three different ways of accidentally asking for greedy decoding when you thought you were sampling.

cells.text: keep one - the first has 0 mass before it

d.title: Three penalties, two arithmetics
d.caption: The first two subtract and the third divides, and that is not a detail — it decides what the number means. A frequency penalty scales with the count, so the fourth occurrence of a token is punished four times as hard as the first; a presence penalty is flat, applied once, however often the token appeared. Repetition penalty is HuggingFace's multiplicative form, where **1.0 means no penalty** rather than zero.
cells: the logit's own size; 1.0 is off

d.title: Almost all of the effect is in the first tenth
d.caption: Greedy decoding at `rp=1.0` produces a loop — 40% unique tokens, the same sentence twice. Raising it to **1.1 takes uniqueness to 0.97**, and 1.2 reaches 1.00. Everything above that changes nothing, because the repetition it was there to prevent has already stopped. The lesson for tuning: this parameter has a cliff near 1.1 and a plateau after it, so sweeping 1.0 to 2.0 in steps of 0.2 mostly measures the plateau.

d.title: What the penalty costs, and why it is less than it sounds
d.caption: The penalised set grows with every token emitted, which sounds alarming until you count it. After 400 tokens only **165 distinct tokens are penalised — 0.328% of the vocabulary**. So the worry that a long generation ends up unable to say common words is not what the arithmetic shows; the real cost is narrower and more specific, which is that the words a passage legitimately needs to repeat get pushed away precisely because it has been using them.
